title: DCB Model
description:
A DCB model: every definition a modeller has authored for one
DCB-based system, in the form the playground exports it. The same
document travels both ways out of the playground, as readable JSON and
as the gzipped payload of a share link.

**There is one kind of fold.** A `projectionDefinition` is it: a value
that starts somewhere and is advanced by the events it handles, over
the query `tag IN (its parameters' arguments) AND type IN (handled
events)`. Declare no parameters and there is no tag, which is what a
global numbering is. Declare one and the same numbering restarts per
tenant.

An **entity property is a binding to one of these**, not a second kind
of thing. `entityDefinitions[].properties` holds `{name, projection}`
entries: the projection declares one parameter typed with the entity's
own identifier, and binding it as a property is what supplies that
argument. Everything the fold needs — the type held, the value it
starts from, the handlers, the script — lives on the projection and
nowhere else, so there is no second place for a type or an initial
value to disagree with the first. The same projection may be bound by
several properties, or read directly by a command, or both.

A lifecycle is not a distinct concept: a modeller who wants one binds
a property named `status` (by convention only) to a projection holding
an ordinary enum custom type. There is no standalone constraint kind:
conditions are inlined into the commands that check them.

**Tags come from value types, not from a separate kind.** Any
`customTypeDefinition` may set `isTag: true`, which is what makes it
an identifier. An entity's own derived identifier is such a value
type — created automatically when the entity is, and from then on
edited exactly like any other value type. A composite value type is
never itself a tag; its tag-ness is derived by looking through it to
whichever of its fields are themselves tag-marked, which is what lets
two unrelated entities share one component (a `TenantId` field) and
be scoped together by it.

**Versioning.** `dcbModelVersion` is what an importer dispatches on;
`$schema` is for editors and is deliberately never read by one. A major
bump means an older reader cannot correctly read the document and must
refuse it; a minor bump means it can, because the addition is one it
ignores. Note that "additive" is judged from the reader's side, not the
schema's: a new member of a closed vocabulary — another condition
operator, operand shape or handler operation — is a *major* change even
though this document merely grows an enum, because a reader that has
never heard of it fails on the value rather than passing it through.

2.0 is such a major. An entity property stopped being a definition of
its own and became a binding; a projection's partition became explicit
in every case; `isOptional` went away, since `null` is an ordinary
initial value of any type and means "no value yet"; and an initial
value may now be a non-empty list. A 1.x reader would misread each of
those rather than ignore it.

4.0 is a major of the subtler kind the reader-side rule exists for:
both of its additions are additive in shape and neither is additive to
a reader. A `PropertyHandler` may carry `via`, so one event type may
now move one projection through several handlers told apart by which
event property names the partition — a 3.x reader would keep only one
of them and fold the wrong value without a word. An `EntityBinding`
may carry `isOptional`, under which an unset identifier binds nothing
instead of erroring — a 3.x reader errors where the author declared
the absence expected. The other direction is safe: a 3.x document says
neither thing, so a 4.0 reader reads it whole.

This schema moves in place for minor changes; a major change is
published at a new `/vN.json` and the old URL keeps serving what it
always served. `x-dcb-schema-revision` moves with every edit either way.

The format is young and the playground it describes is a prototype.
Expect majors.

$schema.description:
The schema this document is written against. Present so that editors
offer completion and inline validation while someone hand-edits an
export; importers must ignore it. Deliberately unconstrained: a
value repointed at a local copy or a mirror — to work offline, or
against an unpublished revision — is a legitimate document, and
pinning it here would turn the one useful thing you can do with this
field into a corruption. What version the document *is* is
`dcbModelVersion`, and only that.

dcbModelVersion.description:
The version of this format, `major.minor`. The only thing an importer
dispatches on. A reader refuses a major it does not know and warns on
a minor newer than its own, which it may read because minors only
ever add what an older reader ignores.

The pattern admits every 4.x rather than pinning one value, because
this schema is edited in place as minors ship and must keep
validating documents written against the earlier ones.

name.description:
What the model is called. Required: an importer can invent a name
for a document that lacks one, but a model called "Imported model"
is a worse outcome than a document that says plainly it is
malformed.

customTypeDefinitions.description:
Value types — either **scalar** (an email string with a pattern,
a money amount, an enum of named members, a tag-bearing
identifier, …) or **composite** (a record of named fields, such
as an order line pairing a product with the price it was
displayed at). An enum is not a distinct form: it is a scalar
type whose `schema` carries the JSON Schema `enum` keyword. A
member reference is still modeled as `{"enumMember": "..."}`
rather than a bare literal, so that renaming a member rewrites
every use of it.

A scalar entry may set `isTag: true`, which is what makes it an
identifier — see `CustomTypeDefinition`. This is also where an
entity's own derived identifier type lives: it is created
automatically alongside the entity (see
`EntityDefinition.identifierType`), and from then on it is an
ordinary entry here, edited, retyped and renamed the same way any
other value type is — the one thing that never changes about it
is that it stays a tag, and it may only be removed by removing
the entity that owns it.

A composite entry — whether entity-owned or standalone — is
never a tag itself; a field of it may be, and one deliberately
shared across several entities' composite identifiers (a
`TenantId` field, say) is what scopes them together.

eventDefinitions.description:
Domain events. An event property whose type is a tag-marked
(`isTag: true`) value type *is* one or more tags on that event,
rendered through that type's `tagSchema`, so
`StudentSubscribedToCourse{courseId: CourseId, studentId: StudentId}`
carries the tags `CourseId:<courseId>` and `StudentId:<studentId>`
(their default `tagSchema`). Tags are never declared separately;
they are derived from property types.

**Tag derivation looks inside composites.** A property typed with
a composite value type contributes one tag per tag-marked field
it contains — a `CourseId` composed of
`{tenant: TenantId, number: CourseNumber}`, both tag-marked,
carries `Tenant:<…>` and `CourseNumber:<…>`, not a tag
namespaced under `CourseId`; a field that is not itself tag-marked
contributes nothing. A *list* of a composite contributes one such
tag **per element** — so
`ProductsOrdered{orderId: OrderId, items: Item[]}` where
`Item{productId: ProductId, price: Money}` carries `OrderId:<…>`
plus one `ProductId:<id>` for every item. This is how a single
event records something that happened to many instances at once.

projectionDefinitions.description:
Every fold in the model — a course's status, a course numbering, a
running total, the set of addresses already registered. Each holds
one value and states its own partition through its parameters.

One partitioned by an entity's own identifier may additionally be
*bound* as a property of that entity (see
`EntityPropertyBinding`); one partitioned by nothing, or by
something else, is read directly by the commands that bind it.
That is a fact about who reads it, not about what it is: the
definition is the same either way.

commandDefinitions.description:
Commands that modelers may issue against the modeled system.
Each command carries a payload (properties), a boundary binding
the entity instances it consults, inline conditions over those
instances, and the events it publishes on success.

scenarioDefinitions.description:
Worked examples: one command, exercised against a log written by
hand, with the outcome the definitions produced frozen beside it.

Scenarios live in the model rather than beside it because a
scenario *is* a reference — to the command it exercises and to
every event its Given is written from — and references are
rewritten in one place. Renaming an event moves it in every
scenario that records it, by the same machinery that moves it in
every handler that folds it.

What a scenario deliberately may **not** do is refuse a change.
Deleting a command a scenario exercises is allowed, and leaves
that scenario broken and saying so. A test reports what a change
broke; it never prevents the change.

projectionScenarioDefinitions.description:
Scenarios asserting what projections fold to, as opposed to what
a command decides. Omitted rather than emitted empty; absent and
empty mean the same thing.

sandbox.description:
The interactive session the export was taken during, if any.
Omitted rather than emitted empty.

EntityDefinition.description:
A modeled thing with an identity and a set of projected
properties.

An entity is projected state, **not** a consistency boundary. It
holds no invariants, handles no commands and decides nothing on
its own. Every decision is made by a command over the instances
it binds in its `boundary` — dissolving the fixed aggregate is
the point of DCB, so an entity is deliberately not one.

An entity derives one identifier type, which *is* serialised —
as an ordinary `customTypeDefinition`, created automatically when
the entity is (scalar, `isTag: true`, a plain string) and named
`identifierType` unless overridden. From then on it is edited
exactly like any other value type: its `schema` may change, it
may switch to `properties` and become composite, it may be
renamed. `isTag` and removability are the two things pinned to
it for as long as the entity owns it — see
`CustomTypeDefinition`.

The derived name is reserved: no other `customTypeDefinition` and
no other entity may claim or derive the same name.

A lifecycle is not a distinct concept here. A modeller who wants
one declares an ordinary property — by convention named `status`
— typed with an ordinary enum value type, exactly like any other
property. Nothing requires an entity to have such a property, and
nothing stops it from having several.

icon.description:
A short glyph — one emoji, or a character or two — that stands
for this entity wherever it is named. Presentation only: no
part of the model reads it, and two entities may share one.
Absent means an authoring tool picks its own placeholder.

identifierType.description:
The name of the entity's derived identifier value type.
Absent means the ordinary case: the name *is* `<name>Id` and
tracks the entity's own name, so renaming the entity renames
its identifier type too. Given once, it stops tracking — the
entity may then be renamed freely without moving it.

This field only ever holds a *name*; the value type it names
is created when the entity is and from then on is edited in
`customTypeDefinitions`, never here — there is no
entity-local schema, fields or tag-schema to author.

properties.description:
The entity's projections, each bound under a local name. An
entry names a `projectionDefinition` and nothing else — what
is held, where it starts and which events move it all live
there.

No entry is reserved: a property named `status` (a
convention, not a rule) is authored, renamed and dropped like
any other. An entity that consults its own tag but projects
nothing beyond it — used purely as a reference — declares no
properties at all.

EntityPropertyBinding.description:
One projection, bound as a property of this entity under a local
name.

The binding carries nothing but the two names on purpose. An
override here — a different initial value, an extra handler —
would be a second place where the mechanics of a fold live, and
the whole point of a property being a binding is that there is
only one.

What makes a projection bindable is its partition: it must
declare exactly one `parameter` typed with this entity's own
derived identifier (or, when scripted, one `argument` of that
type, actually interpolated by its `tagFilter`). Binding it as a
property is what supplies that argument — the instance being
read. A projection with no such parameter is not wrong, it is
just not this entity's property; it is read directly by a
command instead.

name.description:
What this entity calls the projection. Local to the entity:
two entities may bind the same projection under different
names, and a command reads it as `{alias, property: <this>}`.

InitialValue.description:
The value a projection holds before any event has been applied.

`null` is a value of every type and means *no value yet* — it is
not the same answer as `0`, `false` or the empty string, and an
authoring tool must not render or offer it as though it were. It
is the one initial value a list may not hold *inside* it: a list
of nothing-yets says nothing a shorter list does not.

A list-typed projection starts at a list, empty or not, of
values of its own type. An enum-typed one names its member as
`{"enumMember": "..."}` rather than as a bare literal, so that
renaming a member rewrites the reference instead of silently
breaking it.

ProjectionDefinition.description:
One folded value — the only kind of fold in this document.

It declares `parameters`, and whoever reads it supplies the
arguments, which *are* its tags:

  `tag IN (arguments) AND type IN (handled events)`

With no parameters there is no tag, and the query is scoped by
event type alone — which is what a global numbering is. With one
parameter typed with an entity's own identifier, the projection
can additionally be bound as a property of that entity, and the
binding supplies the instance. Nothing in this definition says
which of the two it is: the partition is the same shape either
way, which is why there is one kind here and not two.

**Numbering is not a special case.** `CourseNumbering` is a
projection whose value is set to the `successor` of the id each
`CourseDefined` carried, so the value *is* the next number to
issue at every point in its life — `initialValue` before anything
has happened, `successor(last)` after. There is no separate
generator concept and no read-side operator: a command binds the
projection and reads it like anything else.

An implementation may still answer such a projection with a single
backwards lookup (`ORDER BY position DESC LIMIT 1`) instead of a
scan — a fold whose every handler `set`s from event properties
alone depends only on the last matching event. That is derived
from the handlers rather than declared, so it holds for any
projection written that way.

**The guard.** A command binding a projection contributes that
projection's query to its append condition, exactly as an entity
binding does. For a numbering this is what keeps it monotonic: a
concurrent command that minted from the same projection
invalidates the append.

**Successor.** On an integer, `n + 1`. On a string, the trailing
run of digits is incremented and both the prefix and any
zero-padding are preserved: `"c1"` → `"c2"`, `"c9"` → `"c10"`,
`"c007"` → `"c008"`. The prefix is never declared — it rides on
`initialValue`.

parameters.description:
What partitions this projection. Every parameter is typed
with a tag-bearing value type — one whose leaves resolve to
at least one `isTag` type, scalar or through a composite's
fields — and contributes the tag(s) those types' `tagSchema`
render: one for a tag-marked scalar, one per tag-marked field
for a composite. Whoever binds the projection supplies one
argument per parameter: a command states them outright, and
an entity property binding supplies the instance it was read
for.

**Tag-bearing types only.** A tag is the only thing that can
narrow a query, and only a tag-marked type is a tag. A parameter
typed `integer` could not restrict what the store returns —
it could only discard events after reading them, which is a
predicate, and predicates live in conditions. So "numbering
per year" needs a `Year` entity; that requirement is what
keeps the read cheap.

An empty list is the ordinary case for a global numbering,
and is what makes its query the only kind in this document
that carries no tag.

A **scripted** projection has no parameters. Discarding after
reading is exactly what its code does, so the values it needs
arrive as `script.arguments` instead, and the partition it
would otherwise have derived from parameters is stated
outright in `script.tagFilter`.

valueType.description:
The type of the value held. Never a composite value type:
the operations that advance a projection act on a single
value, and a record of fields has none. A script that needs
to accumulate a record keeps it private and names the one
field a reader sees in `script.exposes`, which is of this
type like anything else.

isList.description:
Whether this holds a list of `valueType` rather than one of
it. A list is homogeneous and never nested — there is no
list-of-lists, and `append` flattens a list-valued operand
rather than nesting it.

initialValue.description:
The value before any event has been applied. Required on a
declared projection and forbidden on a scripted one, whose
`script.initialState` starts it instead.

For a numbering this is the first number issued, and the only
place a prefix is stated.

script.description:
Present when this projection is advanced by code. A script
carries a `tagFilter`: it declares no parameters to derive a
partition from, so the filter is the only thing that can say
what the query reads — empty meaning the whole log, exactly
as no parameters do.

handlers.description:
The handled event types are the projection's query. One event
type may appear on several handlers provided they are told
apart by `via` — see `PropertyHandler` — and every handler
whose guard passes applies, in declaration order; without
`via` an event type appears at most once. Declared handlers
carry an operation and an operand; a scripted projection's
carry one `code` body each.

An empty list is legal and means nothing moves this yet — a
projection mid-authoring reads as its initial value, which is
a more useful thing to show than a refusal to store it.

ProjectionParameter.description:
One or more tags of a projection's query, named so a command can
supply it. `propertyType` must be a tag-bearing value type — an
entity's derived identifier or a standalone one, scalar and
`isTag: true` or composite with tag-marked fields.

ProjectionScript.description:
Code in place of declared handlers, for state whose accumulation
no operation in this vocabulary can express — a window, a running
comparison, anything needing a value the earlier events implied
rather than carried.

**What it costs.** The code is stored and displayed; nothing
parses it, checks it, or rewrites it. A scripted handler is
checked for the event it claims and nothing else, and renaming an
event's property leaves every mention of it inside the code
untouched. That is the price of the escape hatch and it is paid
in full.

**What it deliberately does not cost.** The derived DCB is
unchanged: the query still comes from the handler keys, and the
tags from the binding (entity property) or from `tagFilter`
(standalone). A script may hide how a value is arrived at; it may
never hide what was read to arrive at it.

**The contract.** Each handler body is an expression over
`state`, `event` and `args`, returning the next state. `event`
carries `data` (the payload). `args` holds one entry per declared
argument. Nothing else is in scope, and the same inputs must
produce the same state: a body that consults an ambient clock
would decide one thing and replay another.

initialState.description:
The state before any event. Any JSON value — unlike a
declared projection's `initialValue` this is not typed, because
nothing outside the code ever reads the state whole.

exposes.description:
Which field of the state a condition reads, when the state is
a record. Absent means the state *is* the value.

This is what keeps an accumulator out of the boundary. The
declared `valueType`/`isList` describe this exposed value, so
conditions type-check exactly as they do over a declared
projection, and the bookkeeping the code needs stays private
to it.

arguments.description:
Values the reading command supplies, one entry per name, in
`args` when the code runs. A binding that reads this
projection must supply exactly these — the same "required
here, rejected there" rule `excluding` follows.

An argument is **not a tag** and can never narrow a query:
the store returns the same events either way and the code
discards what it does not want. That is the whole difference
between an argument and a `ProjectionParameter`, and it is
why a parameter must still be tag-bearing.

tagFilter.description:
The tags of this projection's query, one entry each, ANDed.
Written as `TagType:value`, naming a scalar, `isTag: true`
value type — a composite has no tag of its own to name; name
its tag-marked fields' own types individually instead. The
value may interpolate a declared argument as `{name}`, or one
field of a composite one as `{name.field}`.

Required on every script, and empty means the whole log —
the same thing declaring no parameters means. A scripted
projection bound as an entity property scopes itself by
interpolating the identifier-typed argument the binding
supplies; one that never did would fold the same events for
every instance and call them different.

ProjectionArgument.description:
One value a scripted projection asks its reader for. Any type —
an argument reaches the code rather than the query, so the
identifier restriction that governs `ProjectionParameter` does
not apply.

PropertyHandler.description:
How one event type advances one projection. Either declared —
`operation` and `value`, with the vocabulary constrained by the
projection's type: `set` for any type, `increment`/`decrement`
for integers, `append`/`remove` for lists — or scripted, carrying
`code` and neither of the other two.

`via` is the discriminator that lets one event type carry several
handlers. Tag matching is by value, whichever property carries
it, so an event with two properties of one identifier type — an
assignment naming both the new holder and the one replaced —
reaches both partitions, and an undiscriminated handler fires
for both. A handler with `via` applies only where that event
property equals the partition's own identifier; where it is
null (unset), the handler skips. Declared handlers only — a
scripted handler's code already sees the whole event.

via.description:
The event property that must be the one naming this
partition for the handler to apply. Must name a property of
`event` whose type matches exactly one of the projection's
parameters. Absent means the handler applies to every event
of its type the query returns — the only legal form before
4.0, and still the ordinary one.

code.description:
An expression over `state`, `event` and `args` returning the
next state. Present only on a projection that declares a
`script`, and never alongside `operation` — the code is the
operation.

HandlerOperand.description:
Where a handler's value comes from. Resolved while projecting a
single event, so the only things in scope are that event's
properties, the property's own current value, and literals.

SuccessorValue.description:
The value that comes after another — `n + 1` on an integer; on a
string, the trailing run of digits incremented with the prefix
and any zero-padding preserved (`"c1"` → `"c2"`, `"c9"` →
`"c10"`, `"c007"` → `"c008"`).

This is where numbering lives. A projection that sets its value
to `{successor: {eventProperty: courseId}}` holds *the next
number to issue* at every point in its life: `initialValue`
before any event, the successor of the last one issued after. The
alternative — folding to the last id and applying successor at
the read — makes `initialValue` mean two different things
depending on whether anything has happened yet, and lets two
commands reading the same value disagree about it.

Nothing restricts this to projections: an entity property may
take a successor too.

EventPropertyValue.description: A property of the event being handled.

CurrentValue.description:
The property's value before this event is applied — the fold's
accumulator.

icon.description:
A short glyph — one emoji, or a character or two — that stands
for this command wherever it is named. Presentation only: no
part of the model reads it, and two commands may share one.
Absent means an authoring tool picks its own placeholder. The
event this command publishes on success takes this same icon
by default (see `EventDefinition.icon`), which is why setting
one here is usually enough to mark both.

feature.description:
The feature this command belongs to — "Course management",
"Checkout". Commands naming the same feature are presented
together.

It is the one field in this document that the modelled system
does not read. No query, boundary, condition or tag depends on
it, and removing every `feature` changes no behaviour: it
records how a *modeler* grouped their work, on a different
axis from the entities the rest of the model is organised
around.

A feature is therefore never declared. It exists because
commands name it, which is why it costs nothing and why an
empty one is not a thing that can be stored.

boundary.description:
Everything this command reads — entity instances and
projections alike, each under a local alias. **This list is
the command's dynamic consistency boundary**, with nothing
contributed from outside it: the append condition's query is
the union of the bindings' queries, an entity binding
contributing its tag(s) — more than one when its identifier
is composite — restricted to the event types reachable
through the properties the conditions read, a projection
binding contributing its arguments as tags and its handled
types.

Every identifier-typed property of every published event
must resolve to a binding in this list — a command may
not write a tag it did not consult. A property supplied from
a projection binding is exempt, provided that projection
handles the event being published: its query then already
covers every event that could have issued the value, and a
freshly minted identifier has no history to consult. The
exemption is unconditional in the partition — a projection
scoped so narrowly that two partitions can mint the same
identifier is a modelling error of the same class as folding
the wrong event, and is not checked here.

**Coverage follows tag derivation into composites.** Since a
property typed `Item[]` writes one `ProductId:<id>` per element,
coverage is checked against the identifier *leaves* of an
emitted property's type, not its surface: emitting `items`
into `ProductsOrdered.items` is covered by a binding whose
`id` is `{parameterName: items, property: productId}`. Without
the recursion the event carrying the most tags would be the
one checked least.

**Declaration order is the chain.** A binding may draw its
operands from a binding *above* it and never from one below,
so a command can read one thing to learn which thing to read
next. One left-to-right pass resolves the chain, and a cycle
is impossible to write.

**Rounds are derived, never authored.** A binding waits only
for the bindings it actually references, so the number of
round trips to the store is the *depth* of that dependency
graph, not the length of this list: two bindings that both
take their identifiers from the payload are one round, not
two. Each binding's round is `1 + max(round of the bindings
its operands name)`, or 1 when it names none — computable in
the same left-to-right pass, since the list is already
topologically sorted by the rule above.

It is a graph and not a tree: `id` and `excluding` may each
name a different binding, and a binding's arguments may name
several. That is why the structure is
derived and rendered rather than written down as nesting,
which could not represent a binding with two parents without
duplicating it.

**Execution.** The chain reads in rounds, but the whole
command decides as of a single point in the log:

  1. `P` := the position of the last event overall — a
     backwards read of everything, limited to one.
  2. Resolve the bindings round by round, every read
     **bounded at `P`**. Bounding matters: a read past `P`
     could decide on an event that the append condition then
     rejects it for.
  3. Evaluate the conditions over the resolved instances.
  4. Append with the condition
     `query = the union of every binding's query, after = P`.

Because the query covers everything read and `P` precedes
every read, any concurrent change to anything this command
looked at invalidates the append — and nothing else does.

conditions.description:
Conditions over the bound instances, all of which must hold
before any event is emitted.

A condition reading a **fanned-out** alias must hold for
*every* instance that alias bound; an empty set satisfies it
vacuously. The quantifier is not written down — it follows
from the alias being plural.

**Zipping.** When a binding fans out over a list, the elements
of that list stay available to conditions about the instances
it bound, at the matching index:

  an operand rooted at a list that some alias in the *same*
  condition also fans from is read at that iteration's index;
  otherwise it is the whole list.

So with `product` bound over `items[].productId`,
`product.currentPrice equals items[].price` compares each
product against the price submitted *for that product*, while
`items[].price greaterThan 0` — mentioning no alias fanned
from `items` — is an ordinary universal over the list. The
pairing is provenance, not declaration: the operands are
correlated because they came from the same list.

**One fan root per condition.** A condition may quantify over
at most one fanned-out root. Two distinct roots is rejected
rather than read as a cross product: their lengths are
unrelated, nothing in this document can assert otherwise, and
the zipped and crossed readings look identical on the page.

An empty list does **not** mean the command is unguarded: the
append condition is derived from the `boundary`, not from
this list. A command with no conditions at all can still be
strictly serialised — which is what binding a parameterless
projection does to it.

publishes.description:
Events the command emits on success. Each entry binds the
emitted event's properties to operands drawn from the
command's payload, a bound instance's properties, or
literals.

Binding.description:
One thing the command reads. Distinguished by which of `entity`
or `projection` it carries.

ProjectionBinding.description:
One projection the command reads, under a local alias. The alias
defaults to the projection name with a lowercased first letter.

A projection read is a binding rather than an inline operand
because it is a read: it costs a round trip, it takes its place
in the chain when an argument comes from a binding above it, and
its query belongs in the append condition. Leaving it inline
would let a command that reads the store claim in its own
boundary to read nothing.

arguments.description:
One entry per parameter of the projection, keyed by parameter
name; each value is the operand supplying that tag. A
projection with no parameters takes no arguments, and its
query carries no tag.

An argument operand may name a binding above this one, which
is what puts a projection into the chain. It may not resolve
to a list: a projection binding reads one partition, so there
is no fan-out here.

EntityBinding.description:
One entity instance the command consults, under a local alias.
The alias defaults to the entity name with a lowercased first
letter; an explicit alias is only needed when a command binds
two instances of the same entity (e.g. transferring between two
courses).

id.description:
Supplies the instance's identifier — typically a property of
the command payload, but equally a projected property of an
instance bound above this one, or the value of a projection
bound above it.

**A list operand binds many instances.** When the operand
resolves to a list type, the binding covers one instance per
element and contributes one query item each. Reading a list
property of an already-fanned-out alias yields a list of
lists, which is flattened and de-duplicated. Nothing declares
this — it follows from the operand's type.

excluding.description:
One identifier to drop from a fanned-out set. Only meaningful
on a fanned-out binding, and needed when the set is derived
from instances that necessarily include the one being acted
on — rescheduling a course must compare against its
subscribers' *other* courses, and every subscriber is by
definition also in this one.

It narrows the binding rather than the conditions on purpose:
a condition over a fanned-out alias must hold for every
instance, so "except this one" cannot be stated as a
condition without turning it into an implication.

isOptional.description:
The binding may be absent: when its `id` resolves to null —
a derived identifier nothing has set yet, an optional
parameter left unset — it binds zero instances instead of
being an evaluation error. Conditions reading the alias then
hold vacuously (the rule steps aside rather than deciding on
a phantom), and reading a property of it yields null.

Deliberately opt-in: an unset identifier nobody declared
possible stays the loud error it always was, because it is
usually an accident. Only meaningful on a singular binding —
a fanned-out one already binds nothing over an empty list.

arguments.description:
Values handed to the scripted projections this binding reads
through the entity's properties, keyed by argument name.
Required exactly when one of them declares an argument, and
rejected otherwise — the same rule `excluding` follows, and
for the same reason: a field that means nothing here is a
mistake, not a no-op. Two scripted projections asking for the
same name are answered once: they are read through one
binding, at one instant.

The entity's own identifier is never supplied here. It is what
the binding already names, and it reaches the projection as
the identifier-typed argument the property binding fills.

They are supplied, not ambient. A command that consults
time-sensitive state takes the instant as a payload property
and passes it here, so the decision stays a pure function of
its events and its parameters — the same events and the same
arguments always reach the same verdict. An implicit clock
would make replay disagree with the original decision.

They do not touch the append condition. The query still
covers the same tags and the same event types; an argument
decides how the events already read are projected, never
which ones are read.

EventEmission.description:
A command's emission of one event, plus bindings supplying the
event's property values.

parameters.description:
Keys are the event's property names; each value is a
`CommandOperand` describing where the value comes from at
execution time. An *optional* event property's entry may be
omitted; the published event then carries the explicit `null`
there — and writes no tag for it, when the property is
tag-marked.

negate.description: When true the condition holds iff the predicate does *not*.

BinaryCondition.description:
`contains` asks whether a list holds one value; `containsAny` asks
whether two lists intersect, which is how "these two schedules
clash" is stated. Both sides of `containsAny` must be lists of the
same type, and `negate` turns it into "must not overlap".

negate.description: When true the condition holds iff the predicate does *not*.

CommandOperand.description:
Where a value comes from inside a command — its boundary, its
conditions and its event emissions.

ParameterValue.description:
A property of the command payload, optionally reaching one field
inside it.

`{parameterName: items}` is the payload property itself.
`{parameterName: items, property: productId}` is that field of it —
and when the property is a list of composites, the field of *every*
element, in order. The shape deliberately mirrors
`AliasPropertyValue`: one hop, never a path.

property.description:
A field of the parameter's composite type. Only meaningful
when the parameter is typed with a composite custom type.

AliasPropertyValue.description:
Something read through a binding. The alias must appear in the
command's `boundary`.

`{alias: course, property: capacity}` is a projected property of
a bound entity instance. `{alias: courseNumbering}` — no
`property` — is a bound projection's value.

`property` is therefore **required on an entity alias** and
**rejected on a projection alias**: an entity has many values and
no single one to mean, a projection has exactly one and no name
for it. That is the same shape of rule `excluding` and
`arguments` already follow — a field that means nothing in its
position is a mistake, not a no-op.

EnumMemberValue.description:
A member of an enum type — a scalar custom type whose `schema`
carries the JSON Schema `enum` keyword. Modeled as a reference
rather than a bare literal so that renaming a member rewrites
every use of it. `enumMember` holds whatever JSON value that
`enum` array actually contains — a plain string is by far the
common case, but nothing here requires it.

ScenarioDefinition.description:
One command, exercised. `given` is a log written by hand rather
than driven, `when` is the command and the arguments it is called
with, and `then` is what the definitions in this model made of
the two.

**`then` is derived, and stored anyway.** No modeler is asked to
predict it — an authoring tool computes it and freezes it. Storing
it is the entire mechanism: the next evaluation either agrees with
what is written here or it does not, and a disagreement is the
report that some edit changed this command's behaviour. A scenario
whose `then` is not stored can only ever say what a command does
now, never that it changed.

**A scenario is identified by a generated id**, unlike every other
definition in this document, whose name is its identity. Its
`name` is derived from the outcome unless overridden, so two
scenarios of one command may well want to be called the same
thing — and a name that changes when the outcome changes cannot
also be the key everything else refers to it by.

id.description:
Generated, opaque, and never shown. What makes this a scenario
rather than what it is called.

name.description:
What to call this scenario. Absent means it is read off the
outcome — "records StudentSubscribedToCourse", "is refused by
course.status == Existent". An authoring tool freezes the
derived name once a scenario drifts, so the label does not
move under the reader at the moment they are trying to read
the difference.

given.description:
The events that had already been recorded, in order. Empty
when the scenario starts from nothing.

ScenarioGivenEvent.description: One event of a scenario's Given, with the payload it carried.

data.description:
One entry per property the event declares — all of them, and
nothing else. An optional property's entry holds `null` when it is
unset, and an absent entry on an optional property reads the same
way. An event that later gains a *required* property leaves every
scenario written before it *broken*, which is the honest report:
there is no value here to have evaluated with.

arguments.description:
One entry per property the command declares — all of them, and
nothing else. An optional property's entry holds `null` when it is
unset — the explicit spelling of "no value"; an absent entry on an
optional property is read the same way.

ScenarioThen.description:
The outcome, as the definitions produced it when this scenario was
last accepted.

`outcome` is a discriminator rather than a union of two shapes.
Publishing an alternative event when a constraint fails — a
refusal that also records something — is then a change to what a
`rejected` outcome carries, rather than a change to the shape
every stored scenario was written in.

What is **not** kept here is the boundary the command read. It is
derivable, it is large, and every edit to a definition would move
it — so keeping it would turn every scenario into a snapshot of
everything and every edit into a storm of differences. An
authoring tool shows the boundary; it does not assert it.

outcome.description:
`published` when every condition held, `rejected` when one did
not.

events.description:
The events published, in order, each with the payload the
command built. Empty for a refusal — until a refusal is
allowed to record something too.

failedRule.description:
Which condition refused the command, and what it saw. Present
exactly when `outcome` is `rejected`.

data.description: One entry per property the event declares.

ScenarioFailedRule.description:
The condition that refused the command. The values are kept
alongside the text because a rule that still fails, on a different
reading than before, is also a change in behaviour.

index.description: Position of the condition in the command's `conditions`.

text.description:
The condition as it reads — `course.subscriptionCount <
course.capacity`. Stored so a drift can be reported without
resolving the condition again, and so a scenario whose command
was deleted can still say what it used to check.

rightValue.description: What the right-hand side read, or null for a unary predicate.

atInstance.description:
Which instance refused it, when the rule was quantified over a
plural binding — the index of the cart line, the subscriber,
the clashing course. Null when the rule was checked once.

CustomTypeDefinition.description:
A value type — either **scalar** (an email string with a pattern,
a money amount, an enum of named members, …) or **composite** (a
record of named fields, such as an order line pairing a product
with the price it was displayed at).

Exactly one of `schema` or `properties` is given, and the choice
is what makes the type scalar or composite:

  - `schema`     — an opaque JSON Schema describing one value.
  - `properties` — a record of named, typed fields.

A composite's fields are typed against the same universe as
everything else, so a field typed `ProductId` is a real reference:
renaming the entity rewrites it, and tag derivation can see it. A
raw JSON Schema could not offer either — inside one, a tag is
indistinguishable from any other string.

**`isTag`** is what makes a value type an identifier, and it is
meaningful only on the scalar form: a composite is never itself a
tag, no matter how `isTag` reads on it. This is what lets two
unrelated entities share one component (a `TenantId` field on
each of their composite identifiers) and be scoped together by
it — a composite that could opt into being its own tag would
break that sharing. A composite's tag-ness is instead entirely
derived by looking through it: every field whose own type is
`isTag` contributes that field's tag to the whole, exactly as
`eventDefinitions` describes for an event's identifier-typed
properties.

**An entity's own derived identifier** is an ordinary
`customTypeDefinition` like any other — see
`EntityDefinition.identifierType`. It is created automatically
when the entity is, scalar and `isTag: true` by default, and from
then on it is edited here exactly like a standalone value type:
change its `schema`, switch it to `properties`, rename it. The
one thing that stays fixed is that it may not stop being a tag —
an entity that could not be tagged could not be bound in a DCB
query — and it may not be removed directly, only by removing the
entity that owns it.

schema.description: The scalar form — an opaque JSON Schema for a single value.

properties.description: The composite form — the type's fields, in declaration order.

isTag.description:
Whether this value type is represented as a tag — meaningful
only when this is the scalar form. Defaults to `false`: a
value type is an inert record of data unless it opts in.

tagSchema.description:
Template rendering this type's value into its tag, when
`isTag` is true. Interpolates `{type}` (this type's name) and
`{value}` (the value); both are required, in either order,
and nothing else is. `{type}:{value}` — the default — is what
every earlier example in this document assumes; rearranging
it (`{type}={value}`) or restyling it changes what an event
consulting this type writes as its tag, everywhere.

CompositeFieldDefinition.description:
One field of a composite value type. Deliberately **not** a
`PropertyDefinition`: a field is always singular and always
required, and it may not itself be typed with a composite.

All three restrictions exist to keep *zipping* meaningful (see
`CommandDefinition.conditions`). Zipping is index correlation
between a fanned-out binding and the list it fanned from, and it
only holds while the two have the same length:

  - a **list** field would flatten, as list-valued reads off a
    plural alias already do, and a flattened list has a different
    length than the list it came from;
  - an **optional** identifier field would contribute a variable
    number of tags, so a binding fanned from it would be shorter
    than its source;
  - a **nested** composite would need a path operand rather than
    the single hop `{parameterName, property}` affords.

Each is a way for the index to drift silently, with nothing on the
page to show it had.

EventDefinition.description:
What an event carries. `properties` is the payload — the part
somebody emitting the event supplies.

icon.description:
A short glyph — one emoji, or a character or two — that stands
for this event wherever it is named. Presentation only: no
part of the model reads it, and two events may share one.
Absent means an authoring tool picks its own placeholder —
conventionally the icon of the one command that publishes
this event, when exactly one does, and otherwise a neutral
mark of its own.

isOptional.description:
The property may hold no value. `null` is the explicit spelling of
"no value" in every payload — a scenario's Given and When, and a
published event's data alike — and it is never the empty string,
which is an ordinary value. A reader may treat an absent entry on an
optional property as the same null; writers spell the null out.
Combining this with `isList` is a modelling slip the playground
advises against: the empty list already says none.

StaticValue.description:
A literal operand. Declared as a type union rather than a
`oneOf` of separate types: an integer satisfies both `integer`
and `number`, which makes a `oneOf` over both reject every whole
number.

TypeName.description:
A simple type, or a declared value type — scalar (which includes
an enum and a tag-marked identifier) or composite, including an
entity's own derived identifier (`<name>Id` unless overridden,
itself an ordinary `customTypeDefinition`). Every declared value
type shares one namespace, so a name resolves against it.

ProjectionScenarioDefinition.description:
A scenario over what one projection folds to, rather than over what
a command decides: given these events, this projection should have
folded to exactly this value. Where a `ScenarioDefinition` asserts
what a command decides, this asserts what the fold arrives at, which
is the thing a command's decision reads.

**The subject is not written down twice.** A scenario names the one
projection it is about, and `then` is that projection's value — there
is nothing to alias and nothing to tick, because there is only ever
one thing being checked. Asserting several projections over one
Given is several scenarios sharing that Given; an authoring tool can
write them in one gesture, but each is answerable on its own and
drifts on its own.

There is nothing in this shape that knows whether an entity binds
the projection, which is the point: the thing being asserted about
is a projection either way.

These are listed separately from the six definition kinds because a
projection may be checked many times over and owned by no single
definition.

id.description:
Generated, opaque, and never shown — the same identity a
`ScenarioDefinition` carries, and for the same reason: two
scenarios over one projection are told apart by nothing else.

name.description:
What to call this scenario. Absent means it is read off what it
found — "ends up 5". An authoring tool freezes the derived name
once a scenario drifts, so the label does not move under the
reader at the moment they are trying to read the difference.

projection.description: The projection this scenario is about, and the only one it asserts.

arguments.description:
One entry per parameter the projection declares (or per script
argument, for a scripted one), keyed by name. A projection with no
parameters takes none, and reads the whole log.

Unlike a command's `ProjectionBinding`, these are *values* rather
than operands: a scenario has no payload and no boundary to draw
one from, so it states the identifier outright, the same way
`ScenarioGivenEvent.data` states a payload.

given.description:
The events to fold, in order. An empty array is meaningful and
common: it asserts what this projection reads before anything has
happened at all.

then.description:
The value this projection should have folded to — of whatever type
it holds, `null` included, and an array when it holds many. Nothing
here can be checked against the model by this schema alone: a
mistyped value is caught when the model is loaded, not when the
document is validated.

Sandbox.description:
The interactive session someone happened to be mid-way through when
they exported. Not part of the model — it is a walkthrough *of* the
model, kept so that a shared link opens on the same state the sender
was looking at. Omitted entirely when no steps have been run.

steps.description: The commands driven so far, in the order they were driven.

SandboxStep.description: One command drive: which command, and the arguments it was given.

command.description: The command driven — a `commandDefinitions` entry by name.

args.description:
One entry per parameter the command declares. Keys are parameter
names and values are of whatever type the parameter carries, so
this schema checks that the object is there and not what is in
it — the same ceiling `ProjectionScenarioDefinition.then` runs into,
and for the same reason.
